title: Subway Hero

jokes.text: I need some women to attend so it doesn't turn into another giant sausage fest.
jokes.setup: Jack is asking Liz to attend a fundraising dinner for John McCain — framed as a professional request.
jokes.punchline: The real reason is purely cosmetic: to prevent a 'giant sausage fest,' reducing Liz to a prop for optics.
jokes.explanation: Classic Jack move — treating Liz as a utility rather than a person. The bluntness of 'giant sausage fest' in this context is funny because Jack says it with total sincerity. Solid opener that sets tone.

jokes.text: What's the Committee to Reinvade Vietnam?
jokes.setup: Jack mentions the fundraising dinner and asks Liz to come.
jokes.punchline: Liz reads the name of the organizing committee — 'to Reinvade Vietnam' — as if it's a throwaway detail, but the absurdity of the name is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — the name of the committee IS the joke, delivered by Liz as a simple clarifying question. No setup needed; the absurdity is baked into the line. The Committee name also pays off later in the episode as a tag on Tracy's PSA.

jokes.text: C. Nor and I had a falling-out after I switched to another dojo.
jokes.setup: Liz asks if Chuck Norris is one of the cool Republican celebrities.
jokes.punchline: Jack reveals he has a personal history with Chuck Norris (calling him 'C. Nor' with casual familiarity) and that they fell out over a dojo change — treating a martial arts studio switch like a serious social betrayal.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional. 'C. Nor' is a perfect nickname — casual to the point of being a text abbreviation, implying deep familiarity. The 'falling-out over a dojo' is an absurdist detail that reveals an entire unseen world of Jack's life with no wasted words. Totally unexpected, perfectly Jack — wealthy, connected, inexplicably has a dojo. One of the episode's best lines.

jokes.text: I'm saving that money for new humidifiers. The same model that's keeping Larry King alive.
jokes.setup: Liz claims she won't donate money until there's campaign finance reform — a principled excuse.
jokes.punchline: The real reason is mundane (humidifiers), but the specific detail that the model is 'keeping Larry King alive' pivots to dark comedy about Larry King's fragility.
jokes.explanation: Funny on two levels: the specificity of the humidifier purchase undercuts Liz's political posturing, and the Larry King joke is a crisp dark-comedy observation. Economy is strong — two jokes packed into one line.

jokes.text: Food network doesn't have a news show.
jokes.setup: Jack asks if Liz watches the news, incredulous she doesn't know about the subway hero.
jokes.punchline: Liz's response reveals she exclusively watches Food Network — explaining her ignorance and defining her character in one line.
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect character joke. The line does triple duty: it's a punchline to Jack's question, it confirms Liz's food obsession as her dominant personality trait, and the deadpan delivery of an obvious statement ('Food Network doesn't have news') is itself funny. Very high character integration.

jokes.text: Thank you, mayor Bloomberger.
jokes.setup: Dennis is accepting a medal from the Mayor of New York.
jokes.punchline: He mispronounces Bloomberg as 'Bloomberger,' adding a hamburger suffix — revealing his dim-bulb character immediately.
jokes.explanation: A quick, efficient character-establishing joke. 'Bloomberger' is an appropriately stupid malapropism that feels completely organic to Dennis.

jokes.text: Stern rules! Baba booey!
jokes.setup: Dennis is mid-acceptance speech at an official ceremony.
jokes.punchline: He interrupts his own sincere moment to shout Howard Stern fan slogans, completely destroying the decorum.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character moment. The joke works because Dennis cannot contain himself even at his own moment of civic glory. 'Baba booey' as a punchline to an otherwise formal ceremony is a great comedic juxtaposition. The spontaneous self-sabotage says everything about Dennis.

jokes.text: Dennis Duffy, beeper salesman and your ex-boyfriend. And Dateline predator. Exonerated Dateline predator. The whole thing was one big silly misunderstanding. Like the Giuliani campaign.
jokes.setup: Jack reveals the subway hero's identity as Liz's ex.
jokes.punchline: The reveal escalates: ex-boyfriend → Dateline predator → 'exonerated' (Dennis's correction) → 'silly misunderstanding' → compared to the Giuliani campaign. Each beat lands harder.
jokes.explanation: This is a beautifully structured escalating sequence. Each additional detail is worse than the last, and the Giuliani comparison is a perfect button — simultaneously a political joke and a precise calibration of Dennis's magnitude of failure. 'Exonerated Dateline predator' as a self-description Dennis uses with pride is especially strong. One of the episode's top moments.

jokes.text: Jonathan, why don't you put on more of that cologne? — delivered by Jack as a way of dismissing the conversation
jokes.setup: Jack tells Liz to be professional and work with Dennis. Liz is visibly upset.
jokes.punchline: Instead of engaging further, Jack uses a non-sequitur order to Jonathan — clearly a power move to end the discussion and also implying Jonathan wears too much cologne.
jokes.explanation: A good Jack power move — he terminates an uncomfortable conversation by giving a completely irrelevant order to his assistant. The implication that Jonathan's cologne is already too strong adds a layer.

jokes.text: When I say subway, you say hero. Subway. Hero?
jokes.setup: Dennis is being confronted by Liz about appearing on the show.
jokes.punchline: Dennis spontaneously tries to start a crowd chant with just himself and Liz, getting only a confused 'Hero?' in response.
jokes.explanation: Dennis attempting to lead a two-person crowd chant is perfectly in character — delusional self-promotion in the wrong context. The other person's reluctant 'Hero?' makes it.

jokes.text: I now declare this store open for all mankind.
jokes.setup: Dennis is cutting a ribbon at his beeper store opening.
jokes.punchline: The grandiosity of 'for all mankind' applied to a beeper store — an already obsolete business — is absurdly overblown.
jokes.explanation: The Apollo-landing language applied to a beeper store is a great absurdist compression. Dennis's complete lack of self-awareness about the scale of his enterprise versus his rhetoric is perfectly on-brand.

jokes.text: We're like Ross and Rachel, but just not gay.
jokes.setup: Dennis is insisting he and Liz have an 'on-again, off-again thing' like a great TV couple.
jokes.punchline: He references Ross and Rachel, then adds 'but just not gay' — a non-sequitur that reveals his fundamental confusion about Friends while also demonstrating his homophobia.
jokes.explanation: The 'but just not gay' addition is brilliantly wrong — Ross and Rachel are not gay, making this a complete non-sequitur that reveals Dennis has some confused relationship with the show. It perfectly captures his dim-witted, casually offensive worldview.

jokes.text: Dennis singing: '* I just want to rock *'
jokes.setup: Dennis mentions his band as if it were a legitimate path to fame.
jokes.punchline: He performs a single line of what appears to be his band's song — it's embarrassingly simple and delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: The joke is entirely in the content of the song — the lyric 'I just want to rock' is the most generic, unambitious rock lyric possible, and Dennis delivers it like it's profound. Good character beat.

jokes.text: I knew that girl was 18. She told me that her last boyfriend was Asian. And that crap doesn't start until college.
jokes.setup: Dennis defends his Dateline predator appearance, claiming he knew the girl was 18.
jokes.punchline: His 'evidence' is that she told him her last boyfriend was Asian, and he adds the bizarrely confident pseudo-logic that 'that crap doesn't start until college' — a deeply wrong and offensive non-sequitur delivered as ironclad reasoning.
jokes.explanation: This is a great piece of character comedy — the 'reasoning' Dennis employs is so internally consistent yet so completely wrong that it becomes a perfect portrait of delusional self-justification. The racial stereotype deployed as logical evidence is repugnant in a way that's entirely intentional and satirical — the joke is on Dennis's warped worldview. High character integration; only Dennis could say this.

jokes.text: He was a major TV star in the '40s, '50s and the fall of 1972.
jokes.setup: Jonathan is introducing Bucky Bright as a notable Republican celebrity.
jokes.punchline: The career timeline — two decades of success and then 'the fall of 1972' — is a perfectly measured deflation. The specificity of 'fall of 1972' implies a very brief, isolated comeback that was never spoken of again.
jokes.explanation: Exceptionally well-constructed. The rhythm — '40s, '50s' creates an expectation of continuous success, then '...and the fall of 1972' arrives as a perfect comedic brake. The specificity of 'the fall of' (not even the whole year) makes it even better. Economy is outstanding — the whole joke lives in that final clause.

jokes.text: He insists on singing. / He insists on singing.
jokes.setup: Jack asks about Bruce Willis, then Jim Belushi as Republican celebrity options.
jokes.punchline: Jonathan gives the identical answer for both — 'he insists on singing' — as if this is a well-documented, irrefutable problem with both men.
jokes.explanation: The repetition is the joke — the exact same phrasing for two different celebrities creates a running gag in miniature. The fact that 'insisting on singing' is apparently a deal-breaker (and both do it) is a funny celebrity-world detail. Great economy.

jokes.text: Good god. When did the party become so boring? The Democrats have all the good celebrities.
jokes.setup: Jack is struggling to find a notable Republican celebrity.
jokes.punchline: Jack's genuine lament that Republicans lack celebrity appeal, framed as a serious political problem.
jokes.explanation: A solid political observation delivered with Jack's characteristic earnestness. Not particularly original but well-placed and character-appropriate.

jokes.text: Oh, no, sir, I don't vote Republican or Democrat. Choosing is a sin, so I always just write in the lord's name. / That's Republican — we count those.
jokes.setup: Jack asks Kenneth if he'd vote Republican if Bucky Bright told him to.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's sincere religious objection to choosing (he writes in God's name) gets immediately co-opted by Jack's cynical 'That's Republican — we count those.'
jokes.explanation: This is among the episode's best jokes. Kenneth's answer is a perfect character moment — sincere, naïve, and funny on its own. But Jack's immediate pivot — 'That's Republican, we count those' — is a devastating political joke that works on multiple levels: it's cynical about how religion and politics intertwine, it's perfectly in-character for Jack, and the delivery implies this is just a known fact. High quotability and rewatch value because it rewards attention.

jokes.text: And an inside monogrammed pocket, you know, for your opium pipe and your switchblade.
jokes.setup: Bucky is waxing nostalgic about elegant men's fashion of the old days — ties, hats, tailored suits, carnation in the lapel.
jokes.punchline: The list of elegant details abruptly ends with 'opium pipe and your switchblade' — delivered as if these were equally standard accessories of refined men.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed misdirection. The setup builds genuine nostalgic atmosphere — 'ties and hats...tailored suits...carnation in your lapel' — so the arrival of 'opium pipe and switchblade' as natural accessories of elegant gentlemen is a perfect subversion. The casual tone ('you know, for your...') makes it land harder. One of the episode's standout lines.

jokes.text: I'm sorry — what now? / Say, why don't you show me around the old studio?
jokes.setup: Bucky drops 'opium pipe and switchblade' as if normal.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's stunned 'I'm sorry — what now?' is the straight-man reaction beat, and Bucky immediately changes the subject rather than address it — implying he's said something he perhaps shouldn't have.
jokes.explanation: The reaction beat extends joke #19. Kenneth's scandalized reaction and Bucky's pivot to changing the subject squeezes additional comedy from the setup. The quick subject change implies Bucky knows he slipped up, which deepens the characterization.

jokes.text: 400% of my sodium? I should not be eating these.
jokes.setup: Liz is in the hallway, apparently eating a snack.
jokes.punchline: She reads the sodium content, acknowledges she shouldn't eat it, and (implicitly) keeps eating anyway — a perfect Liz Lemon moment of self-aware self-destruction.
jokes.explanation: A compact Liz character beat. The '400%' specificity is good, and the joke lands because we know she's still going to eat them. High character integration.

jokes.text: Ladies and gentlemen, I give you the bravest New Yorker since Bernie Goetz, Mr. Dennis Duffy.
jokes.setup: Dennis is being introduced on TGS as a hero.
jokes.punchline: He's compared to Bernie Goetz — the vigilante subway shooter who shot four Black teenagers in 1984 — a deliberately inappropriate comparison that subverts the heroic framing.
jokes.explanation: A sharp dark joke. Bernie Goetz is a deeply ambiguous figure whose status as a 'hero' was fiercely contested along racial lines, so invoking him as the standard of NYC bravery is a loaded, pointed comparison. The show commits to the darkness without winking.

jokes.text: It's the Stanley Cup, honey. It's hockey's ultimate prize. And me and it, we're teaming up to fight illiteracy.
jokes.setup: Someone asks about the trophy Dennis is carrying.
jokes.punchline: He's somehow obtained the Stanley Cup and has appointed himself and it as a team to fight illiteracy — an absurd project announced with complete confidence.
jokes.explanation: 'Me and it, we're teaming up to fight illiteracy' is a great line — the human-trophy partnership, the vagueness of 'fight illiteracy' as a celebrity cause, and the 'honey' address to someone who asked a simple question all work together. Good absurdist Dennis moment.

jokes.text: I've watched seven different people die in subway stations.
jokes.setup: Someone says they wouldn't have had the guts to do what Dennis did.
jokes.punchline: Toofer's response isn't inspiring — he's not claiming he would have helped. He's watched SEVEN people die and did nothing, delivered with complete matter-of-fact NYC detachment.
jokes.explanation: A well-observed joke about NYC detachment culture — watching seven people die and treating it as a personal metric of resolve. The specificity of 'seven' is perfect; it implies an actual running count.

jokes.text: All I could think about was Derek Jeter. And it was like, check this out, Jeter, you think you're better than me?
jokes.setup: Dennis is asked what was going through his mind during the heroic act.
jokes.punchline: Rather than describing courage or instinct, Dennis reveals his inner monologue was a rivalry with Derek Jeter — an unhinged motivation that has nothing to do with heroism.
jokes.explanation: This is the best Dennis joke in the episode. The setup asks for genuine insight into a heroic moment; the answer reveals a petty, delusional inner world where Dennis is in direct competition with Derek Jeter. 'Check this out, Jeter, you think you're better than me?' captures Dennis's psychology perfectly — he saved a life as a point in a personal rivalry with a Yankees legend who has never thought about him. Exceptional character integration.

jokes.text: Uh, why is this movie called 'The Hours' when it feels so much longer? They should call this thing 'The Weeks'.
jokes.setup: Jenna is in the middle of a serious conversation about Liz's relationship with Dennis.
jokes.punchline: She randomly pivots to complaining about the movie 'The Hours,' comparing its runtime to 'The Weeks' — a non-sequitur that reveals she's been thinking about this the whole time.
jokes.explanation: A good non-sequitur that breaks the emotional moment. 'They should call this thing The Weeks' has good economy and the beat where Liz absorbs this is implied comedy.

jokes.text: Reaction beat: Liz processes 'The Weeks' comment in silence.
jokes.setup: Jenna pivots to complaining about 'The Hours' in the middle of giving Liz relationship advice.
jokes.punchline: The pause before the scene continues implies Liz is silently absorbing the bizarre topic change — a beat of shared confusion.
jokes.explanation: The beat after the joke matters but isn't a distinct laugh — it's a tag. Functional.

jokes.text: Dennis is like those off-brand Mexican Cheetos. My 'Sabor de soledad'? I only have Spanish delis in my neighborhood.
jokes.setup: Jenna is trying to warn Liz about Dennis using a food metaphor.
jokes.punchline: Liz instantly knows exactly what product Jenna means — 'Sabor de soledad' (Flavor of Loneliness) — and explains why she has them, confirming she eats them regularly. The name 'Sabor de soledad' is both funny and poignant.
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly crafted joke with layers. 'Sabor de soledad' (Flavor of Loneliness) as a fake brand name is inspired — it perfectly captures the existential bleakness of off-brand junk food. Liz immediately recognizing it, and explaining she only has Spanish delis, simultaneously confirms she eats garbage and reveals details of her neighborhood with no wasted words. One of the episode's best lines. High character integration.

jokes.text: Tracy. My friend. Have you ever considered becoming the celebrity face of the Republican party?
jokes.setup: Jack needs a celebrity for the Republican dinner and has turned to Tracy.
jokes.punchline: The specific choice of Tracy Jordan — chaotic, impulsive, financially reckless — as the ideal face for a political party is inherently absurd.
jokes.explanation: The setup for a longer political comedy thread. Works as a scene-setter.

jokes.text: Black people supporting Republicans? Does hot support cold? Does rain support the earth?
jokes.setup: Jack asks Tracy to be the face of the Republican party.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's rhetorical questions escalate from 'hot/cold' (a standard opposites metaphor) to 'does rain support the earth' — which is actually TRUE, making his argument accidentally collapse.
jokes.explanation: Tracy's logic self-destructs mid-argument, which is perfect — 'rain does support the earth' is actually correct, so his examples contradict his point. Whether this is intentional by the writers or a happy accident, it works as Tracy-level reasoning.

jokes.text: Do you like lower taxes? / If I paid taxes, I sure would.
jokes.setup: Jack tries to find common ground with Tracy on Republican issues.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's response — 'If I paid taxes, I sure would' — is an admission that he doesn't pay taxes, delivered with total unapologetic confidence.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Tracy line — the conditional 'if I paid taxes' is delivered without shame as if it's a perfectly reasonable qualifier. The structure is impeccable: Jack's setup leads to an expected 'yes' answer, and Tracy gives a 'yes' that implies something much worse. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: How about gun ownership? / Go on.
jokes.setup: Jack continues running through Republican positions as selling points.
jokes.punchline: 'Go on' — Tracy's intrigued response implies he's very on board with gun ownership and wants to hear more.
jokes.explanation: 'Go on' as a two-word response to 'gun ownership?' is extremely economical. The implication is clear, delivered with minimum fuss. Good economy.

jokes.text: And let none of us forget the GOP is the party of Lincoln. / Lincoln was a Republican? / Actually, today's Republican party would be unrecognizable to Lincoln. He fought a war to preserve federal authority over the states. That's not exactly small government. / Dotcom, this need you have to be the smartest guy in the room is... off-putting.
jokes.setup: Jack uses the 'party of Lincoln' argument. Tracy is genuinely surprised.
jokes.punchline: Dotcom enters with a historically accurate and politically pointed correction, which Jack deflects not by disagreeing but by criticizing Dotcom's social behavior.
jokes.explanation: Multi-layered political comedy. Tracy's genuine ignorance of Lincoln's party is funny; Dotcom's historically accurate (and politically devastating) correction is funnier; and Jack's response — ignoring the substance to attack Dotcom's personality — is the perfect evasion. The joke works on three levels simultaneously and each escalation is better than the last.

jokes.text: I guess that's why I'm still single.
jokes.setup: Jack says Dotcom's need to be the smartest person in the room is 'off-putting.'
jokes.punchline: Dotcom accepts this entirely and connects it to his romantic life — revealing surprising self-awareness and vulnerability.
jokes.explanation: A good character button. Dotcom's self-aware response adds a poignant note without dwelling on it. Economical.

jokes.text: Damn. The Republican party sounds pretty attuned to my unique way of life.
jokes.setup: Jack has pitched states' rights, guns, and lower taxes.
jokes.punchline: Tracy synthesizes these as being 'attuned to his unique way of life' — the joke being that his 'unique way of life' involves not paying taxes, owning guns, and presumably operating outside normal civic structures.
jokes.explanation: Tracy's phrase 'my unique way of life' implies a rich, unspecified chaos that the audience fills in. Good character line.

jokes.text: For five bucks I will.
jokes.setup: Bucky is reminiscing about his old dressing room. He starts telling a story about what he used to do there.
jokes.punchline: He trails off and says 'For five bucks I will' — the rest of the story is unclear, but the implication is extremely seedy. The joke is entirely in what's left unsaid.
jokes.explanation: Magnificent economy. We get no information and yet complete information — 'for five bucks I will' in the context of his dressing room implies a dark and specific history. The joke is entirely in the implication, and the cut-off makes it funnier. One of the episode's most efficient jokes.

jokes.text: Hey, dummy, I was just telling these dummies how we used to go in the park and make fun of all the joggers.
jokes.setup: Dennis is hanging out backstage with the TGS crew.
jokes.punchline: He addresses Liz as 'dummy' and refers to the crew as 'these dummies,' then describes a leisure activity of mocking joggers — revealing his worldview that exercise is inherently mockable.
jokes.explanation: The 'dummy' address establishes Dennis's condescending familiarity. Mocking joggers as recreation is good character color.

jokes.text: Oh, I'm gonna run in a circle, so I can live longer.
jokes.setup: Dennis is describing how they'd mock joggers.
jokes.punchline: His impression of a jogger's internal monologue reduces running to a circular, vain act — which is actually a coherent critique of cardio culture delivered with contempt.
jokes.explanation: A decent anti-exercise joke. Dennis's contempt for self-improvement is funny and consistent.

jokes.text: Hold on a second. Who orders a salad from a burger joint? You watching your figure there, sweetheart? What, are you gearing up for swimsuit season?
jokes.setup: Someone in the TGS crew has ordered a salad.
jokes.punchline: Dennis launches into unsolicited fat-shaming/body commentary directed at a woman in the group — the joke is how quickly and instinctively he pivots to this, revealing his casual sexism.
jokes.explanation: The joke is mostly about Dennis's awfulness — his instinct to body-police women. Functional but not particularly crafted.

jokes.text: Very funny. / Very funny? How would you know?
jokes.setup: Liz says 'very funny' in a sarcastic, dismissive tone.
jokes.punchline: Dennis snaps back with 'How would you know?' — a mean-spirited retort that implies Liz can't recognize humor.
jokes.explanation: Sharp comeback, but more mean than funny. Economy is excellent — four words doing a lot of damage. Slightly below average for the episode.

jokes.text: We used to call this 'the jew room.'
jokes.setup: Bucky is showing Kenneth around the old studio with nostalgia.
jokes.punchline: He casually reveals an antisemitic nickname for one of the rooms as a piece of innocent historical color.
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Bucky says it with zero awareness that it's offensive — the casualness is the point. It's a satirical comment on the open bigotry of the 'good old days' that Bucky is nostalgically praising. The economy is perfect — just four words dropped in the middle of a tour.

jokes.text: Hey, chief, the kid's birthday party that hired the Urkel impersonator is down around the hall.
jokes.setup: Bucky Bright is being shown around the studio in his old-fashioned attire.
jokes.punchline: A crew member mistakes Bucky for an Urkel impersonator hired for a birthday party — conflating two completely different eras of Black TV culture and implying Bucky's style reads as costume rather than genuine.
jokes.explanation: A decent visual joke — the crew member's casual misdirection adds another layer of indignity to Bucky's visit. The 'Urkel impersonator' detail is specific enough to be funny.

jokes.text: Are you gonna cry? / Yeah, he's gonna cry.
jokes.setup: Bucky appears to be on the verge of emotional reaction to being mistaken for an impersonator.
jokes.punchline: Dennis and the crew immediately begin mocking the old man's potential tears — revealing the pack mentality Dennis has created.
jokes.explanation: Weak joke — mostly just mean. The comedy is below the episode's average and relies on bullying an old man without a strong enough punchline.

jokes.text: Elizabeth Conworthy Lemon. / Okay, that's not my middle name.
jokes.setup: Dennis is about to launch into a dramatic confrontation with Liz.
jokes.punchline: He gets her middle name completely wrong. Liz's flat correction deflates the drama immediately.
jokes.explanation: The 'full name' dramatic confrontation is a familiar trope; subverting it by having Dennis get the middle name wrong is a good deflation. The same joke pays off later at 14:29 — making this a setup for a callback.

jokes.text: Entertaining a guest of the show is called being professional. It wasn't a date or whatever — I paid for dinner.
jokes.setup: Jenna confronts Liz about a tabloid photo of her and Dennis having dinner.
jokes.punchline: Liz's 'defense' — 'I paid for dinner' — inadvertently confirms the date while trying to deny it, and implies she always ends up paying for Dennis.
jokes.explanation: Liz's inadvertent self-betrayal is nicely done. The 'I paid for dinner' detail confirms what she's denying and adds a new layer of sadness.

jokes.text: He can't get credit cards, Jenna, because his cousin Teddy used Dennis' social to get a cell phone that Teddy then couldn't pay for because this Indian guy that he was working for... You know what, I don't have to explain myself to you.
jokes.setup: Jenna says 'You always paid for Dennis.'
jokes.punchline: Liz launches into an elaborate backstory explaining why Dennis has no credit — going deeper and deeper into the story before catching herself and refusing to continue.
jokes.explanation: This is a great character joke — Liz knows the full backstory of Dennis's credit history in exhausting detail, proving she's more embedded in his chaotic life than she admits. The fact that she stops herself mid-explanation, having already revealed too much, is perfectly timed. The escalating detail (cousin Teddy → cell phone → couldn't pay → 'this Indian guy') implies the rabbit hole goes much deeper.

jokes.text: I just wandered around the building all night. I didn't run into another single living soul, except one gigantic lesbian.
jokes.setup: Kenneth asks where Bucky went after being shown out earlier.
jokes.punchline: He spent the entire night wandering the building alone — and the only person he encountered was 'one gigantic lesbian,' delivered as if this explains everything.
jokes.explanation: The payoff of Bucky having wandered 30 Rock overnight is absurd enough, but the specific detail of 'one gigantic lesbian' — delivered as the only notable fact — is the kicker. It implies an entire unwitnessed story that we'll never hear.

jokes.text: Who is Conan O'Brien, and why is she so sad?
jokes.setup: Bucky encountered someone while wandering the building, described as a 'gigantic lesbian.'
jokes.punchline: That person is revealed (via his question) to be Conan O'Brien — Bucky doesn't know who Conan is, and thinks Conan is a woman.
jokes.explanation: A masterful joke. The callback reveals that the 'gigantic lesbian' was Conan O'Brien — the show is set at 30 Rock, where NBC's Late Night was filmed. Bucky doesn't recognize Conan AND thinks he's a woman. The additional 'why is she so sad' implies Conan's legendary melancholy/anxiety, known to insiders and audiences alike. Every word does work. Highly quotable and gets a huge laugh from comedy-savvy viewers.

jokes.text: It's purgatory, Tracy. / Richard Nixon? / I can't believe I'm dead. There was still so much left on my bucket list. So many different kind of buckets I wanted to own. Buckets.
jokes.setup: Tracy appears to have a vision or hallucination of purgatory where he encounters Richard Nixon's ghost.
jokes.punchline: Tracy mishears 'bucket list' as a literal list of buckets — then says 'Buckets' as if that itself is a solemn conclusion.
jokes.explanation: Tracy's literal interpretation of 'bucket list' is a perfect Tracy Jordan joke — he hears 'bucket' and immediately goes to a world where he has a sincere wish to own many types of buckets. The trailing 'Buckets.' as a final solemn word is the best part. High character integration.

jokes.text: We've lost some prestige because of the Bush administration. / And Watergate. / I'm trying to keep that on the DL around here.
jokes.setup: Nixon's ghost is recruiting Tracy for the Republican party and lamenting lost prestige.
jokes.punchline: Tracy brings up Watergate; Nixon asks him to keep it quiet — as if reputation management still matters to his ghost.
jokes.explanation: The joke of Nixon's ghost still trying to keep Watergate 'on the DL' is a solid piece of political absurdism — the denial and image management continues even in death.

jokes.text: Black, Jewish, one eye, a white wife. It was a big tent back then, Tracy.
jokes.setup: Nixon's ghost is telling Tracy about Sammy Davis Jr. as an example of Republican diversity.
jokes.punchline: Nixon lists Sammy's characteristics — each one a minority identity — as evidence of the party's inclusivity, with the deadpan 'big tent' conclusion.
jokes.explanation: The list of Sammy Davis Jr.'s identities — each a distinct form of difference — delivered as a checklist for inclusion is sharp political comedy. The 'big tent' phrase is used genuinely but the accumulation makes it ironic.

jokes.text: I got a mission.
jokes.setup: Nixon and Sammy Davis Jr.'s ghosts ask Tracy to restore the GOP's 'big tent.'
jokes.punchline: Tracy's flat, determined 'I got a mission' after being convinced by Nixon's ghost in purgatory is a great straight-faced absurdist button.
jokes.explanation: Works as a button to the purgatory sequence. Economy is high; three words summarize Tracy's entire character arc in this subplot.

jokes.text: Social conservative, fiscal liberal.
jokes.setup: Jack asks Dennis about his politics.
jokes.punchline: Dennis gives a coherent-sounding political taxonomy that is exactly the wrong combination — socially conservative (restrictive of others) + fiscally liberal (spending other people's money) while not paying taxes himself.
jokes.explanation: A superb two-word character joke. Dennis sounds like he knows political terminology, but his self-described stance is the exact opposite of principled — 'fiscal liberal' when you don't pay taxes is maximally ironic. Perfect economy.

jokes.text: I don't like a lot of people, Jenna, but that dumb creep makes me laugh.
jokes.setup: Jenna expresses exasperation that Liz had fun with Dennis.
jokes.punchline: Liz's defense of Dennis is simultaneously an admission that she has limited social connections, an insult to Dennis ('dumb creep'), and a genuine expression of affection.
jokes.explanation: A nicely layered line that does character work and comedy simultaneously. 'Dumb creep' as a term of endearment captures Liz perfectly.

jokes.text: Do I? I might be an idiot. I know I'm supposed to make myself nice meals, instead of eating junk.
jokes.setup: Jenna says Liz 'knows better' than to date Dennis.
jokes.punchline: Liz's 'I might be an idiot' — genuine self-interrogation rather than defense — is funny because she's actually genuinely unsure.
jokes.explanation: A small but genuine character beat. Liz's self-doubt is funny because it's sincere — she's actually entertaining the possibility. The food metaphor continuation keeps it in the episode's thematic register.

jokes.text: Do you know what I use my oven for? / Warming your jeans in the morning? / That's right, and it feels good.
jokes.setup: Liz says she knows she should make herself nice meals instead of eating junk.
jokes.punchline: When Liz asks what she uses her oven for, Jenna immediately guesses 'warming your jeans' — meaning she knows Liz so well that she can correctly identify this. Liz confirms it proudly.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed joke. The setup ('what do I use my oven for?') implies a standard 'I don't cook' punchline, but 'warming your jeans in the morning' is unexpected and specific enough to be genuinely funny. The fact that Jenna knows this instantly, and Liz confirms it with 'and it feels good,' adds a layer of sad warmth. High character integration — this could only be Liz Lemon.

jokes.text: My cologne is distilled from the bilge water of Rupert Murdoch's yacht.
jokes.setup: Dennis tells Jack he 'smells rich' and Jack thanks him.
jokes.punchline: Jack explains that his cologne is literally made from the yacht bilge water of his boss Rupert Murdoch — an absurd flex that implies intimate access to Murdoch while being revolting.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's single best line. 'Bilge water of Rupert Murdoch's yacht' is perfect on every level: bilge water is repulsive boat waste, yet Jack wears it as a status symbol; it implies a specific and disturbing closeness to Murdoch; and it's delivered with complete sincerity. The joke captures Jack's entire character — the obsession with power, the perverse status signaling, the relationship with Murdoch as both employer and demigod. Exceptional originality, economy, and character integration. Highly quotable, demands rewatch.

jokes.text: And when I grab on, I do not let go. Like a killer whale going nuts on his trainer at Sea World.
jokes.setup: Dennis tells Jack he's 'in' with Liz now.
jokes.punchline: He compares his romantic persistence to a killer whale attacking a SeaWorld trainer — an image that is both violent and absurd, delivered as if it's a compliment.
jokes.explanation: A great Dennis metaphor — he means it as a declaration of loyalty but the comparison to a killer whale attack reframes it as threatening obsession. The specificity of 'going nuts on his trainer at Sea World' adds texture.

jokes.text: Love is hiding who you really are at all times, even when you're sleeping. Love is wearing makeup to bed and going downstairs to the Burger King to poop, and hiding alcohol in perfume bottles. That's love.
jokes.setup: Liz says 'Isn't that what love really is?' about not having to try with Dennis.
jokes.punchline: Jenna's definition of love is a cascading list of deeply unhealthy relationship behaviors delivered with total conviction — each item stranger and more disturbing than the last.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's very best jokes and a strong candidate for the show's all-time great character moments. Each item in Jenna's definition of love is worse than the last — hiding who you are → makeup to bed → using Burger King as a secret bathroom → hiding alcohol in perfume bottles. The structure is perfect escalation. It's completely specific to Jenna's deranged romantic life and reveals everything about her character. The deadpan 'That's love' button is the perfect closer. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: If you give into it, you just start to feel kind of numb and warm, and then you just get sleepy. That's not that bad. / That's exactly what they say it's like when you freeze to death.
jokes.setup: Liz describes the comfortable numbness of settling for Dennis.
jokes.punchline: Jenna points out that Liz's description matches the physical process of freezing to death — a devastating and precise reframe.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed joke with genuine emotional resonance. The setup is Liz trying to rationalize a bad relationship; the punchline perfectly and clinically diagnoses it as self-destruction. Jenna's response works as dark comedy, relationship commentary, and a devastating character insight simultaneously. The structure is impeccable — Liz's description genuinely does match freezing to death, making the comparison exact rather than hyperbolic. One of the episode's standout lines.

jokes.text: Blurgh.
jokes.setup: Jenna has just compared being with Dennis to freezing to death.
jokes.punchline: Liz's single non-word response — 'Blurgh' — is her signature expression of defeated self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: 'Blurgh' is Liz Lemon's signature expression — a single made-up word that captures her entire emotional state. As a reaction to the freeze-to-death comparison, it's perfect. Maximum economy (one word) with maximum character specificity.

jokes.text: You wanted to do something private with another man, it wasn't gay. No, it was just two men celebrating each other's strength.
jokes.setup: Bucky is showing Kenneth old photos of himself 'with the boys' from the old studio days.
jokes.punchline: He preemptively clarifies that whatever they were doing 'wasn't gay' — then describes it in a way that sounds exactly like gay intimacy.
jokes.explanation: The classic 'that's not gay' joke done well — the redefinition Bucky offers ('celebrating each other's strength') sounds like a euphemism that describes exactly what he's denying. The period-specific context (men of that era being in denial) adds satirical weight.

jokes.text: Nixon's ghost convinced my ghost to help the GOP. God bless that wiretapping bastard.
jokes.setup: Tracy returns from his purgatory vision with a new mission.
jokes.punchline: He describes the ghost-on-ghost recruitment as fact, then refers to Nixon as 'that wiretapping bastard' as a term of endearment.
jokes.explanation: 'God bless that wiretapping bastard' is a great line — an affectionate tribute to Nixon that simultaneously acknowledges his crimes. The casual acceptance of all this as normal Tracy experience is well-handled.

jokes.text: I can't talk now. I gotta get my wallet out of the toaster.
jokes.setup: Jack wants to discuss the campaign commercials right away.
jokes.punchline: Tracy ends the conversation because he needs to retrieve his wallet from the toaster — implying he put it there, and this is apparently urgent.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Tracy exit line. The wallet-in-the-toaster situation implies an entire unseen domestic chaos without explanation. It's delivered as a completely mundane urgent errand, which makes it funnier. One of the episode's most quotable lines.

jokes.text: Elizabeth Sarah Lemon — / That's not my middle name.
jokes.setup: Dennis attempts to propose with a dramatic full-name address.
jokes.punchline: He gets her middle name wrong again — 'Sarah' this time instead of 'Conworthy' — and Liz's flat correction is the same as before.
jokes.explanation: The callback pays off beautifully — Dennis uses a different wrong middle name for his marriage proposal, confirming he never knew her middle name and hasn't even tried to find out. Liz's identical flat response deepens the running gag. The proposal context makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Will you marry me? / Oh, god.
jokes.setup: Dennis pulls out a ring and proposes marriage.
jokes.punchline: Liz's 'Oh, god.' is the entire response — not a refusal yet, just the sound of someone whose worst nightmare is materializing.
jokes.explanation: 'Oh, god.' as a reaction to a marriage proposal is a great beat — it's not even a word, just an involuntary noise. Pure character.

jokes.text: You don't know this guy. He is not the man you think he is.
jokes.setup: Dennis is proposing publicly, presumably to cheers from bystanders who see the 'subway hero.'
jokes.punchline: Liz's desperate address to the crowd — 'He is not the man you think he is' — while literally true (he's a Dateline predator) plays as a rom-com cliché in reverse.
jokes.explanation: Good ironic inversion of the typical 'give him a chance' crowd moment. The fact that Liz is 100% correct makes it funnier.

jokes.text: I could get any girl here I want. And not just the fatties and the butterfaces.
jokes.setup: Dennis is angry at Liz for rejecting him publicly.
jokes.punchline: His attempt to reassert his desirability by specifying that his options extend beyond 'fatties and butterfaces' makes everything worse — the qualifier implies that those are his default.
jokes.explanation: The self-undermining brag — claiming you have options beyond your usual type — is a classic Dennis move. The cringe factor is high.

jokes.text: Shut up, crowd. I command you as the subway hero — shut up.
jokes.setup: Dennis is trying to propose over crowd noise.
jokes.punchline: He invokes his hero status as authority to command a crowd to be quiet — treating 'subway hero' as an ongoing official title.
jokes.explanation: Great character joke — Dennis believes being a subway hero confers ongoing civic authority. 'I command you as the subway hero' is a perfect line for his delusion of grandeur.

jokes.text: You know, a stripper offered to give me a squeezer last night. A white stripper.
jokes.setup: Dennis claims he doesn't need Liz because he has options.
jokes.punchline: He cites a white stripper's offer as evidence of his desirability — the 'white stripper' specification as a status clarification is the key absurdist detail.
jokes.explanation: The racial specification as a quality marker is a very Dennis-specific detail — it reveals his worldview without editorial comment.

jokes.text: I'm the loser. I guess I'm the one who totally missed catching the puck at that Islanders game.
jokes.setup: Liz calls Dennis a loser. Dennis disputes this with 'Oh, I'm the loser?'
jokes.punchline: His evidence that Liz is the loser: she missed catching a puck at an Islanders game. This is his most damning piece of evidence.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'that Islanders game' (implying Dennis was there and remembers this with bitterness) is excellent. The fact that this is Dennis's strongest counter-argument reveals everything about his value system.

jokes.text: And so do all New York based sports teams.
jokes.setup: The argument between Liz and Dennis escalates through 'You suck / No, you suck.'
jokes.punchline: Dennis expands his 'you suck' accusation to encompass all New York sports teams — a surreal escalation that broadens the scope of his grievances.
jokes.explanation: A good escalation — the petty argument suddenly balloon-expands to include all of New York sports. Dennis's pivot reveals that this is also about something else, something deeper, involving the Islanders specifically.

jokes.text: My fellow blackmericans— / Can I just say black Americans? There's no such thing as blackmericans.
jokes.setup: Tracy is about to deliver his Republican PSA.
jokes.punchline: He invents the portmanteau 'blackmericans,' which Jack calmly corrects — but the word itself and Tracy's confidence in deploying it is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Tracy's accidental portmanteau and Jack's patient correction is a great beat. 'Blackmericans' is a terrible word, which makes it funnier that Tracy says it with conviction.

jokes.text: My fellow black Americans, Dr. King once had a dream, a dream that we all share: To build a 200 foot high wall to keep Mexico out. And he also hated the estate tax.
jokes.setup: Tracy begins his Republican PSA by invoking Martin Luther King Jr.
jokes.punchline: Dr. King's dream is falsely completed as 'a 200-foot wall to keep Mexico out' and 'he also hated the estate tax' — a satirical demolition of how politicians invoke MLK to support opposite positions.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top three jokes. The structure is perfect: invoke MLK with full ceremony ('a dream that we all share'), then complete it with a hard-right immigration position. The second beat — 'he also hated the estate tax' — delivered as a flat afterthought, is equally strong. The joke is a surgical critique of appropriating civil rights rhetoric for opposite political ends. Tracy's earnestness makes it land harder. Exceptional originality.

jokes.text: I get it. The Republican party means less taxes, more guns, and the end of the gun tax.
jokes.setup: Tracy expresses second thoughts about being the Republican face.
jokes.punchline: He summarizes his Republican understanding as 'less taxes, more guns, and the end of the gun tax' — the third item ('gun tax') is completely invented and redundant, showing Tracy thinks guns are specifically being taxed and that this is the party's top priority.
jokes.explanation: Tracy's summary is good because it starts coherent ('less taxes, more guns') then adds the invented 'end of the gun tax' — implying he thinks there's a specific gun tax he's been personally burdened by. Good Tracy logic.

jokes.text: No matter what, blackmericans are gonna always vote Democrat. / They will, won't they? / Unless... black people, don't vote. Just don't do it.
jokes.setup: Tracy realizes no matter what, Black voters will vote Democrat.
jokes.punchline: His solution is simply voter suppression — 'black people, don't vote. Just don't do it' — presented as an innovative campaign strategy.
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly dark political joke. Tracy arrives at voter suppression as a logical marketing solution, treating it as a practical business problem. The buildup — 'Unless...' followed by a long pause — gives the punchline full impact. The joke works as satire of real voter suppression tactics framed through Tracy's naive logic. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: In the amount of time it'd take for you to vote, you could play three games of pool. Three. And that's fresh.
jokes.setup: Tracy is now actively making his anti-voting PSA.
jokes.punchline: He offers as a concrete alternative to voting: three games of pool. The 'Three.' restatement for emphasis and 'that's fresh' as a sign-off compound the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: The pool alternative to voting is perfectly absurd, but 'Three.' as an emphasized repetition and 'that's fresh' as a closing slogan push this into great territory. It sounds like actual terrible political messaging, which is the whole joke.

jokes.text: I'm Tracy Jordan, and I improve this message. Paid by the committee to reinvade Vietnam.
jokes.setup: Tracy finishes his PSA with a standard political sign-off.
jokes.punchline: He says 'I improve this message' instead of 'I approve' — a Tracyism. And the funding credit is 'the committee to reinvade Vietnam,' the absurd entity from the episode's opening.
jokes.explanation: A perfect button to the PSA sequence. 'I improve this message' as a Tracyism on the standard political boilerplate is excellent, and the callback to 'the committee to reinvade Vietnam' from the episode's opening pays off the earlier setup. The episode's running political absurdism reaches its apex here.

jokes.text: Now if you'll excuse me, Nixon asked me to take some stuff out of his Wikipedia page.
jokes.setup: Jack thanks Tracy for making a difference.
jokes.punchline: Tracy exits to do Nixon's Wikipedia editing — as if this is a natural post-purgatory follow-up task, and as if Nixon's ghost has ongoing Wikipedia concerns.
jokes.explanation: Excellent absurdist button. Nixon's ghost having active Wikipedia concerns is a great contemporary-meets-historical joke. The matter-of-fact delivery of 'I gotta take some stuff out of his Wikipedia page' is perfect economy.

jokes.text: Dennis is off the show. I booked the 911 bird. Winston dialed 911 with his beak and said fire, but only because he didn't know the word for rape.
jokes.setup: Jack tells Liz he's bumping Dennis from TGS.
jokes.punchline: The replacement is a bird who called 911, but the bird's motivation is darkly clarified — it said 'fire' because it didn't know the word for rape.
jokes.explanation: This might be the episode's most audacious joke. The setup (heroic bird) is instantly subverted by the implication that the bird witnessed something terrible and could only express it within its limited vocabulary. 'But only because he didn't know the word for rape' is a shocking, precisely calibrated dark joke that lands on a knife's edge. The originality is exceptional — no other show would write this, and very few writers would think of it. Near the very top of the episode.

jokes.text: Well, when we sobered up, we realized we'd eaten the peacock and we put the ham in Pat Weaver's office.
jokes.setup: Bucky is telling Kenneth a story about the old days at NBC.
jokes.punchline: The story involves eating the NBC peacock (the network's mascot) while drunk, and storing a ham in the president's office.
jokes.explanation: The story of eating the peacock mascot is a great NBC-specific detail. Pat Weaver (Sigourney Weaver's father) was a legendary NBC president — the name-drop grounds the absurdity in real TV history. The juxtaposition of 'ate the peacock' and 'put ham in Weaver's office' as a two-part drunk adventure is well-constructed.

jokes.text: Now if you'll excuse me, I'm off to Chinatown to pick up some human growth hormones so that Mr. Jordan's tigers don't realize that he's aging.
jokes.setup: Jack tells Kenneth that things 'get weird' sometimes.
jokes.punchline: His example of 'weird' is that he personally goes to Chinatown for human growth hormones to administer to Tracy's tigers so they don't notice Tracy aging.
jokes.explanation: Another exceptional joke. This is a universe-building moment — the revelation that (1) Tracy keeps tigers, (2) Jack personally manages their pharmaceutical needs from Chinatown, and (3) the specific concern is that the tigers will notice Tracy aging, implies that these tigers are acutely aware of their owner's mortality and this is a live concern. Every layer of this joke is absurd and specific. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Oh my... there's your weird.
jokes.setup: Jack leaves to get HGH for Tracy's tigers, just as he told Kenneth that things get weird.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth encounters 'the weird' immediately — presumably seeing something (the bird, or another bizarre thing) and confirming Jack's point.
jokes.explanation: Works as a button but isn't a standalone joke. The setup does more work than the punchline here.

jokes.text: It seems like all that stuff you said came true. I am a loser. My mall appearance got canceled. The mighty ducks are mad at me because I left the Stanley Cup on a water taxi.
jokes.setup: Dennis comes to find Liz after being bumped from the show.
jokes.punchline: His evidence of being a loser is a cascade: mall appearance canceled + left the Stanley Cup on a water taxi. The specific image of the Stanley Cup abandoned on a NYC water taxi is perfect.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the Stanley Cup pays off perfectly — he lost it on a water taxi. The Mighty Ducks being specifically mad at him (a real NHL team) is a good detail. The accumulation of losses is well-paced. 'Left the Stanley Cup on a water taxi' is a standout image.

jokes.text: I can only imagine the classic song I'm gonna write after this.
jokes.setup: Dennis is at his emotional lowest, having lost everything.
jokes.punchline: In his darkest moment, he pivots to imagining his future band glory — the heartbreak as creative fuel.
jokes.explanation: A good callback to the band subplot. The implicit joke is that his 'classic song' will sound like 'I just want to rock.' The self-mythologizing in the face of total collapse is very Dennis.

jokes.text: Oh, well this one's dating a Dateline predator. Exonerated. And we're not dating.
jokes.setup: Bucky is telling Kenneth a story about a girl he knew.
jokes.punchline: He refers to Liz's situation as 'this one's dating a Dateline predator' — and Liz's dual correction ('Exonerated. And we're not dating.') is a running gag callback.
jokes.explanation: The 'exonerated Dateline predator' running gag pays off well with Liz making both corrections simultaneously. It's become a double-correction reflex.

jokes.text: Boy, that's one mouthy sandwich girl, isn't it?
jokes.setup: Liz corrects Bucky about her relationship status.
jokes.punchline: Bucky dismisses Liz by calling her a 'sandwich girl' — the antiquated term he revealed earlier in the episode — now applied to a professional woman, revealing his unchanged worldview.
jokes.explanation: Good callback — 'sandwich girl' is paid off by being applied to Liz, whom Bucky categorizes by the old studio hierarchy. The dismissal of Liz as 'mouthy' while calling her by the sexist old term is pointed satire.

jokes.text: It was on a subway platform just like this. On a night just like this. / It's still daytime. And we're inside.
jokes.setup: Dennis is beginning to tell the story of his heroic subway act in dramatic fashion.
jokes.punchline: His cinematic framing — 'a night just like this' — is immediately destroyed by Liz's flat factual corrections.
jokes.explanation: A very well-constructed deflation. Dennis's movie-trailer framing ('on a night just like this') is clinically dismantled by 'It's still daytime. And we're inside.' The double correction — time of day AND location — is perfectly deployed.

jokes.text: You failed the firefighter exam? / Yeah, it's totally biased against the Irish, you know.
jokes.setup: Dennis mentions he failed the firefighter exam among his life regrets.
jokes.punchline: His explanation — the exam is biased against the Irish — is a completely unfounded conspiracy theory delivered with total certainty.
jokes.explanation: Irish bias in the firefighter exam is a great Dennis conspiracy — the NYPD/FDNY historically having many Irish-Americans makes this a particularly specific and absurd inversion. His certainty is the key.

jokes.text: If reality TV has taught us anything, it's that you can't keep people with no shame down.
jokes.setup: Liz is trying to encourage Dennis despite his fall from grace.
jokes.punchline: The encouragement is framed entirely in reality TV logic — the shameless thrive on television — which is both a commentary on Dennis and on reality TV culture.
jokes.explanation: An excellent observational joke with genuine satirical bite. 'You can't keep people with no shame down' is a sharp commentary on celebrity culture and reality TV, delivered as sincere encouragement. Highly quotable and applicable beyond the episode.

jokes.text: Dennis, don't you dare. / Liz, work with me now. Just go limp. / It'll be phenomenal, Liz, come on. / Ah, damn, it's the wrong track. It's stupid express. / You thought it was this track too, didn't you?
jokes.setup: Dennis tries to recreate his heroic subway act — pushing Liz onto the tracks — as a publicity stunt.
jokes.punchline: He picks the wrong track (the express), the attempt fails, and then he implicates Liz by noting she was looking at the same track — suggesting she'd anticipated he'd try this.
jokes.explanation: A great escalating physical comedy sequence. 'Just go limp' is a superb line — Dennis has thought through the logistics of shoving Liz in front of a train. 'It's stupid express' as his complaint about the wrong train is a perfect absurdist frustration. 'You thought it was this track too, didn't you?' is a terrific button that implicates Liz in the scheme.

jokes.text: You'll be back, Liz Lemon. You'll be back. / You'll be back, dummy.
jokes.setup: Liz walks away from Dennis saying 'Never again.'
jokes.punchline: Dennis shouts after her — 'You'll be back, Liz Lemon. You'll be back' — and then refines the goodbye to 'You'll be back, dummy' as she disappears.
jokes.explanation: A good closing character beat. The adjustment from 'Liz Lemon' to 'dummy' as she walks away is the joke — he switches back to his default nickname mid-declaration of confidence. Ends the episode on a perfect Dennis note.

tmdb_overview: Dennis becomes a New York City celebrity after jumping in front of a train and saving someone who fell on the tracks. Meanwhile, Jack desperately tries to persuade Tracy to become the celebrity face of the Republican Party.
insight: Subway setting fuels 66 jokes in 24 minutes, anchoring character comedy to absurdist New York observations.
